transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in today?

Hi, yeah. Um, so my supervisor told me I had to come see someone because... well, I work on the line over at the packaging plant, and I keep leaving my station. Like, I'll just pop up and walk away when I'm supposed to stay put. Or even in our morning shift meetings, I just take off before I even think about it. He says it's becoming a huge safety problem. 

Which, I mean, I guess I get it, because last week this guy Jimmy—he drives the forklift on the floor—almost backed into a massive pallet of those blue sports drinks. Have you ever had those? They taste like straight cough syrup, I honestly don't know how people drink them. My little brother loves them though, he buys them by the case at the dollar store. But anyway, Jimmy is always not looking where he's going, so if I'm walking around... wait, what was I saying? 

Oh, right, yeah, my boss is mad because I just can't seem to stay in my spot. I just get up and go without thinking about it first.
Have you noticed this kind of impulsive, can't-stay-put behavior and trouble focusing since you were a kid, or is this something that's only started recently?

Oh, no, it's always been like this. Definitely since I was a kid. Even back in elementary school, I was always the kid who just... could not stay in my seat. I’d just get up and start wandering around the room. We had this class pet in third grade, a hamster named Barnaby, and I’d always go over to his cage because he was on this little wheel that squeaked constantly. It was so loud, and the teacher, Mrs. Gable—she had this really big hair, like huge, I don't even know how much hairspray she used every morning—she would get so mad at me. 

I was always talking over her and just blurting things out in the middle of her lessons. She sent so many notes home to my mom about me wandering off or talking out of turn. My mom used to stick them on the fridge with this magnet from a pizza place that closed down a few years ago. Man, I miss their pizza. It had those little pepperonis that curl up into little cups and get all crispy on the edges, you know? The grease would just pool right in the middle of them. It was the best. But yeah, I've always been getting in trouble for getting up and blurting stuff out, ever since I was little.
Aside from this lifelong pattern, have you recently had a period of several days where you felt unusually elevated, euphoric, or irritable, along with needing much less sleep than usual?

Elevated? Like... super happy or something? No, I don't think so. And I definitely need my sleep. I mean, I'd sleep more if I could, but the guy in the apartment next to mine just bought this massive subwoofer for his TV. It literally shakes the walls. I actually had this picture of my dog, Buster—he’s a pitbull mix, the absolute sweetest thing, he totally thinks he’s a lap dog even though he weighs like seventy pounds—and the bass from the neighbor's TV vibrated the wall so hard the frame fell off and completely shattered on the floor. 

I had to sweep up glass for like an hour because I was terrified Buster would step on a piece and cut his little paw. Vet bills are so ridiculously expensive right now. My friend took her cat in just for a stomach thing last month and it cost her like four hundred dollars. Can you believe that? Four hundred dollars! For a cat! She works at the dollar store with my brother, so she really didn't have the extra money for it, but what are you gonna do, just let your pet be sick? 

But um... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, feeling elevated and not sleeping. Yeah, no, I don't get like that. I just get regular tired.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a lifelong (since elementary school) pattern of hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (leaving seat/workstation inappropriately, blurting out, difficulty staying still) combined with clear inattentive features (marked distractibility, tangential/derailed speech, losing track of conversation topics, difficulty sustaining focus). Symptoms began in childhood, have persisted into adulthood, and currently cause significant occupational impairment and safety concerns at work. Mood elevation, decreased need for sleep, and other manic symptoms were explicitly denied, ruling out a manic/hypomanic episode. The combination of both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptom clusters, each meeting sufficient symptom count and chronicity, supports ADHD, Combined Type.
